title: hyprfocus.json
description: The hyprfocus declaration: what may exist on the desk, per mode. One `base` declares the whole desk; each mode states only its difference from it. This is a materialisation model, not a permission model — a resource a mode does not admit is not loaded, so there is nothing to ask permission about. Deltas are a writing convenience with no runtime existence: a resolver folds base + mode into one complete desk BEFORE anything acts on it, because applying deltas incrementally against a running system would make the result depend on the order they were applied. Read by the compositor, the shell and the CLI; written by the shell's mode panel.

version.description: Declaration format version. Bumped when the grammar changes incompatibly.

modes.description: Every mode, keyed by id. `neutral` is the resting state and must exist.

id.description: A stable kebab-case identifier. Names the thing, not the file that happens to implement it, so moving code does not change a declaration.

desk.description: A complete desk: every resource that exists, named. This is both the shape of `base` and the shape a resolver produces.

workspaces.description: Workspaces that exist and are reachable. Admitted by enabling their workspace rule; withdrawn by disabling it, with any windows on them held.

bindings.description:
Binding trees UNDER MODE CONTROL — the ones a mode may withhold. A tree not named here is always available and no mode can remove it.

The default is deliberately 'available', because the two mistakes cost wildly different amounts. A tree missing from this list means a mode does not take away as much as it meant to. A tree wrongly removed means a desk with no terminal and no way back to another mode, which is a reboot. So a mode names what it takes, never what it keeps.

`root` and the modes tree are refused whatever a declaration says: root carries the leader key, and the modes tree is the only way into another mode.

services.description: Background tasks that run, named from the scripts contract's task map rather than as raw units — so the declaration says what work happens and the contract says which units implement it.

projects.description: Projects open on their scene's workspace, named from the projects store.

scenes.description: Scene definitions, keyed by the workspace name they arrange. Geometry only — a scene never decides whether its workspace exists. A scene is admitted implicitly with its workspace; per-mode scene substitution is deliberately not in version 1.

notify.description: Notification routing, keyed by resolved source id (never by the self-reported application name). `default` applies to anything unmatched.

requires.description:
Hard composition edges, keyed by `kind:name`: what a resource CANNOT FUNCTION without. The resolver takes the transitive closure, so a mode that admits `project:obsidian` gets what it needs without listing it. A mode that explicitly `remove`s something required is a conflict the resolver reports.

This expresses composition only. Ordering, readiness and failure handling between the units of one capability belong in the unit files, where systemd already does them better than a resolver could.

Mirrors systemd's `Requires=`. Prefer `wants` unless the resource is genuinely broken without the dependency.

wants.description:
Soft composition edges, keyed by `kind:name`: what a resource USES but can run without. Pulled in by default like `requires`, but a mode may drop it and the resolver honours that silently rather than reporting a conflict.

This is the common case and the one to reach for first. Obsidian without its indexer is degraded, not broken — so a media mode can keep the window and stop the indexing to reclaim resources, which is behaviour that already ships today.

Mirrors systemd's `Wants=`.

verdict.description: What a notification does on screen. History records every notification with the verdict applied to it regardless — suppression governs what interrupts, never what is knowable afterwards.

revocation.description: What happens to a resource a mode stops admitting. `hold` parks it out of sight and restores it when the mode ends; `retire` stops it and does not bring it back. Holding buys attention, retiring buys capacity — so windows usually hold and services usually retire.

blocks.description: Ordered groups of window classes sharing the workspace.

barred.description: Classes that legitimately open here without belonging to a block. Barred because auto_group grabs whatever opens while a group holds focus.

classes.description: Literal class or Lua pattern, matched literal-first so a hyphenated class does not trip on `-` being a quantifier.

order.description: Position in the left-to-right sequence. With a layout provider this is the order boxes are placed, not a correction applied afterwards.

group.description: All matching windows live in one Hyprland group, so the block is a single tile however many windows it holds.

share.description: Fraction of the work area this block holds.

collect.description: Members that drifted to another workspace come home. Off by default: a window moved away deliberately should stay where it was put.

guard.description: How a non-group block resists being grouped. `deny` also refuses a deliberate toggle, for a tile whose job is to be a fixed region beside a group.

delta.description:
A change to one resource kind. `only` is exclusive and replaces the base's set; `add` and `remove` apply against it. The two forms are mutually exclusive, because a declaration that said both would have no single obvious meaning.

`only` and `remove` differ in how they meet a requirement. `only` says what to inherit, so the requirement closure may still add to it. `remove` is an explicit statement that a resource should not be there, so a requirement that contradicts it is a conflict the resolver reports rather than silently resolving either way — silently starting it ignores what you said, and silently omitting it breaks whatever needed it.

notify.description: Routing overrides merged onto the base's, keyed by source id. `default` sets the fallback for this mode.

revoke.description: Per-resource revocation overrides for this mode, keyed by resource id.

presentation.description:
How the desk looks while this mode runs. Passed through by the resolver untouched; the shell owns its meaning.

`palette` is a LEASE, not a write (LEO-288): while the mode runs the desk shows this palette, and when it ends the baseline (the sun's, or the user's pick) comes back untouched. Omit it and the mode tints nothing — `accent_role` already picks a role within whatever palette is active, and this optional field is for the rare mode that must pick a different palette altogether.

`wallpaper` leases by the same rule (LEO-289): a mode that needs a specific look behind it names the file; the mood's own binding still wins, and an absent name leases nothing.

palette.description: The palette leased while this mode holds. Must name a variant the shell carries (Theme.qml / a theme pack); an unknown name reads as no lease — resolution never fails.

wallpaper.description: The image bound while this mode holds. Names a file in the wallpaper directory (absolute paths and the mood/palette bindings remain the broader contract); an unknown name reads as no lease.

ref.description: A resource reference, `kind:name` — `workspace:`, `binding:`, `service:`, `project:`. Singular, and qualified because requirements cross kinds: opening a project pulls in the background work it needs.
